implementation_notes: datetime.date is the date-only type (no time, no zone; date.today() and date.fromisoformat() are the boundary APIs) but the standard library has no interval type, so the idiomatic realization is a frozen dataclass holding from_date and a nullable until with __contains__ and overlaps methods - frozen=True plus eq gives value semantics and hashability, and __post_init__ is the natural place for the non-empty-period invariant. Two facts define the Python form: date and datetime do not compare with each other (a TypeError, not a silent False), and naive and aware datetimes do not compare either - so one period type must use one of the three consistently and convert only at the boundary. Where large tables of validity windows are queried analytically, pandas' Interval/IntervalIndex (closed on either side, half-open by default) is the library route, but that is a storage and analysis choice rather than a different realization of the pattern.
pitfalls: datetime.date and datetime.datetime are not comparable (TypeError), and aware versus naive datetimes raise as well: one period type must be used consistently, with conversion at the boundary only.
date.fromisoformat accepts only full ISO forms (no reduced precision) and validates shape, not meaning; parse lenient input with an explicit parser and raise with the offending value.

An in-memory invariant is not enforced by the database: without a unique/exclusion constraint on (identity, from_date), two sessions can insert overlapping periods even though the dataclass refuses to build one.
